outline.description: To understand the appellate court's decision in *Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp.*, one must first navigate the specific factual matrix and procedural history that gave rise to the dispute. The litigation began not in federal district court, but before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB), an administrative body within the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) tasked with resolving disputes over trademark registration. Understanding these foundational principles is essential for grasping why the court affirmed some aspects of the TTAB's decision while vacating others. outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Analysis of DuPont Factor Two – Similarity of Goods/Services
outline.description: In *Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp.*, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit addressed the foundational inquiry of trademark infringement: whether the parties' goods or services are so similar that consumers would likely mistake one for the other. Under Section 2(d) of the Lanham Act, a refusal to register occurs if "confusion is likely." To determine this likelihood, courts apply the thirteen factors established in *Application of E. I. Du Pont de Nemours & Co.* (the *DuPont* factors). While all thirteen factors inform the ultimate legal conclusion, each individual factor represents a specific question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence. outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: Vacatur Regarding DuPont Factor Six – Market Crowding and Scope Protection
outline.description: In *Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp.*, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit addressed a critical procedural and analytical flaw within the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board's (TTAB) application of the *DuPont* likelihood-of-confusion test. Specifically, the court examined how the Board analyzed the sixth *DuPont* factor, which concerns "the number and nature of similar marks in use on similar goods." The central holding of this chapter is that a failure to maintain consistency in defining "similar goods" across different *DuPont* factors can lead to an artificial inflation of a mark's commercial strength, thereby distorting the market-crowding analysis.
